doc.title: Terri Lyne Carrington interviewed by Monk Rowe, Toronto, Canada, January 9, 2003

title: Being a bandleader, sideperson and producer
summary: She says leading and touring are impractical financially, and that she mostly works as sideperson, having produced Dianne Reeves's That Day.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: Record labels, producers and the business of making albums

blocks.x: Let me ask you about being a band leader. How practical is it these days to try to put a band together, and tour in support of an album perhaps?

It’s not very practical. It was very difficult to do. You figure out how you can do it and you decide how much you can invest into your career and hope that you are contributing to your longevity in the long run. But I don’t think if you’re trying to get rich you should be a leader or tour in support of yourself unless you’re having just a huge amount of success at the time, and then you have to get in there and milk it.
Right. I would guess that part of your life is juggling: being a side person, being a producer, trying to do your own recordings. Is that true?

Yes I think right now I’ve been juggling mainly just being a side person and doing some things as a leader. I haven’t been doing much producing lately. I would love to do more, it’s something I really do enjoy. I did produce a record for Dianne Reeves called “That Day” and I’m very proud of that record and it was nominated for a Grammy award as well. But I haven’t really done much since then.
